chapter_theme: Songs at Tiruporur (the heading reads திருப்பேரூர், the songs திருப்போரூர்): three confessions of bondage to women, one naming the courtesans' messengers, betel and greed, end in a plea for grace or for the feet, and a fourth song is a litany of epithets for Murugan, the sun that clears the darkness of ego.
structure_note: 710 to 712 are confessions about women; 713 is praise alone, a chain of Sanskrit epithets.

710.reading: The poet tells how women with honeyed speech feign great infatuation, send hundreds of messengers in a day, call a man home, laugh and flirt, embrace him, bend to give betel and bite it halfway, drink the saliva of his lips as honey and play many games, all meaning to snatch his wealth through his infatuation, and asks for grace so that his desire for these sinful women leaves him. The praise names the hero who, carrying off the hunter girl, won with one sword against the hunters who surrounded him, the nephew of Vishnu who sent his discus by thought to the elephant seized in the lotus pond, and the lord of Tiruporur with its chariots, walls and towers.
710.nuance: நீள்பொருள் பறிப்பார்: the whole performance, messengers and betel included, is aimed at wealth, which is what makes these courtesans in the Kural's sense. The sword fight with the hunters is a less common detail of the Valli story.

711.reading: The poet calls himself a great sinner whose heart runs to the women with arrow-eyes, mountain breasts, crescent foreheads and cloud-dark hair, and wears their net of pleasure, and asks for grace so that he is spared the disgrace of dying in the dullness and folly that cover him. The praise names Murugan son of the lord who wears erukku, thali and thumbai flowers and the Ganga, who dwells in the tongues and hearts of those who praise him in Vedic verse, whose vel destroyed Sura in the sea, and Valli's partner at Tiruporur.
711.nuance: அசட்டால் மூடுகின்ற மசக்கால் மாயும் இந்த அவத்தால்: what the poet fears is a pointless death in stupor, more than the women themselves. இருக்காலே நினைந்து may mean 'by the Rig Veda' or 'with the verses'.

712.reading: The poet describes the women he roams beside, swan-gaited and peacock-graceful, moon-faced, honey-tongued, with breasts like Meru, carp eyes and bamboo shoulders, and asks that by Murugan's grace he fall at the feet on which Sama Vedic priests and gods strew fresh flowers. The praise names Murugan who embraced the girl guarding the field on the hunters' hill, the cause who spoke the Agamas, Vedas and Puranas, the compassionate one whose vel churned the sea to mud against Sura, worshipped by Brahma, Vishnu, Uma and Siva, at Porur.
712.nuance: The description of the women is a catalogue of conventional likenesses, part for part, and takes half the song. வினாமிக is obscure to me.

713.reading: A song of praise alone: Murugan is the sun that destroys the darkness of ego in the poet's dark and foolish mind, the sun of the three worlds, the son of Siva and nephew of Narayana, the child given by Uma under her many names (Kumari, Syamala, Amali, Yamala, Purani, Narayani), Guha, Saravana, the jewel desired by the hunters' daughter, the lord of the six sects and their gods, worshipped by all worlds and all Vedas at Samarapuri.
713.nuance: ஆணவ திமிரமே அரி சூரிய: the one doctrinal phrase makes Murugan the sun that removes anava, the first of the bonds. சமய மாறிரு தேவத சமய நாயக reads as lord of the six sects. Many of the compound epithets in the middle (பமர பாரப்ர பாருண, பசுர பாடன பாளித) are Sanskrit I can't divide with confidence. சமர மாபுரி translates the shrine's name, போர் being battle.

links.note: 710 shows the whole performance of feigned infatuation (மாமயல் உடைத்தார் போலவும்): messengers by the hundred, the embrace, betel bitten halfway, all to snatch the man's wealth (நீள்பொருள் பறிப்பார்). Kural 913 calls the embrace of women of wealth false (பொய்ம்மை முயக்கம்), like embracing a stranger's corpse in a dark room. The Kural judges the embrace; the song shows the staging that makes it false.

713 opens by naming Murugan the sun that destroys the darkness of anava (ஆணவ திமிரமே அரி சூரிய) in the poet's dark mind. Tirumanthiram 117 says the malas end before the sun appears (சூரியன் தோற்றமுன் அற்ற மலங்களே), as the sunstone burns cotton only in the sun's presence. Both use the sun's coming as the figure for the bond removed, in Tirumular the guru, in 713 Murugan.

713 praises Murugan as the lord of the six sects and their gods (சமய மாறிரு தேவத சமய நாயக), worshipped by all worlds and all Vedas. Tirumanthiram 1533 says those who saw the six sects did not see him, and he is not the thing the six sects hold (ஆறு சமயப் பொருளும் அவனலன்). On the reading that 713 makes the Lord the object the sects reach, the two disagree; if 713 means only that he rules over them, the gap narrows.

source_issues: Chapter heading reads திருப்பேரூர், but the songs name திருப்போரூர் (710, 711), போரி மாநகர் (712) and சமர மாபுரி (713); the heading should probably be திருப்போரூர்.
